To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) resistance testing is useful for guiding treatment decisions for all HIV-positive individuals, (ii) resistance testing is particularly useful when starting a new antiretroviral regimen and when switching to a new antiretovirial regimen, and (iii) resistance testing is not useful for monitoring virological response to treatment or for monitoring for drug resistance
resistance testing should be performed when the patient is failing a regimen, when the patient has a history of treatment failure or when a patient has a history suggestive of poor adherence.

resistance testing should be done in the following situations: 1. when starting antiretroviral treatment in a patient who has been exposed to a single drug or drug class; 2. when starting antiviral therapy after a virologic rebound; 3. when starting antireroviral therapy in a patient who is failing a regimen with multiple drug classes, and 4. when switching to an alternative regimen in a patient with a viral load below 50 copies/ml.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

genotypic resistance tests are most useful when the decision to change antiretroviral therapy (ART) is based upon a change in viral genotype, or a significant change in the viral load or CD4 cell count.

resistance tests should be performed in patients who are failing therapy, but that the results of the test should be used to guide therapy decisions only if the results can be interpreted and the results are used to guide therapy.

resistance testing is useful and should be performed at the following times: when the HIV RNA load is above the threshold for resistance testing (i.e., >5000 copies/mL); in patients who have failed a previous antiretroviral treatment regimen; and in patients who have a history of poor adherence.

genotypic resistance tests can be useful to determine the best antiretroviral regimen to use, but they are not useful to determine whether or not to initiate antiretrovirus.

the use of genotypic resistance tests in clinical management is not only cost-effective, but can also be used to optimize the treatment of patients, and thus improve the clinical outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
resistance tests are not just for patients who are failing therapy.
the use of resistance tests should be based on a clear understanding of the limitations of the test and the clinical context in which the test is being applied.
